clinicalPearls: The vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation is a congenital arteriovenous fistula between choroidal or quadrigeminal arteries and the persistent embryonic median prosencephalic vein of Markowski, not a true aneurysm of the mature vein of Galen.
The neonatal form presents with high-output cardiac failure that is disproportionate to any structural cardiac lesion, driven by the massive intracranial left-to-right shunt.
A loud cranial bruit audible over the fontanelle or orbits in a neonate with heart failure is a valuable clue.
Because so much combined ventricular output is diverted to the low-resistance shunt, there may be retrograde diastolic flow in the aorta and compromised systemic and coronary perfusion.
Later infantile presentation is dominated by macrocephaly, hydrocephalus and developmental delay rather than cardiac failure.
The melting brain phenomenon reflects chronic cerebral venous hypertension and hypoperfusion causing progressive parenchymal loss.
Staged endovascular embolisation, timed to balance cardiac stability against neurological maturation, is the mainstay of treatment.
A validated neonatal scoring system incorporating cardiac, cerebral, respiratory, hepatic and renal function guides whether to intervene urgently or defer.
reference.pathophysiology: The malformation arises early in gestation from a persistent arteriovenous shunt draining into the median prosencephalic vein, the embryonic precursor that normally regresses as the internal cerebral veins form. Persistent high-flow shunting dilates this venous sac and diverts a large fraction of cardiac output through a low-resistance circuit. In the neonate this imposes a huge volume load, producing high-output biventricular failure, pulmonary hypertension and a diastolic steal that impairs systemic organ perfusion. Within the brain, impaired venous drainage raises cerebral venous pressure, causing hydrocephalus, impaired cerebrospinal fluid resorption, and chronic ischaemic injury with calcification and atrophy.
additionalDifferentials: structural congenital heart disease causing neonatal heart failure
other cerebral or hepatic arteriovenous malformations
persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
additionalInvestigations: catheter cerebral angiography to define feeding arteries and drainage
echocardiography for shunt burden and pulmonary pressure
B-type natriuretic peptide and cardiac biomarkers
renal and hepatic function panels for multi-organ effect
redFlags: neonatal high-output cardiac failure refractory to medical therapy
cranial bruit with rapidly increasing head circumference
signs of raised intracranial pressure or seizures
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the severity of cardiac failure and the degree of established brain injury at presentation; neonates with intractable heart failure or extensive parenchymal loss fare poorly, whereas selected infants treated by staged embolisation can achieve good neurodevelopmental outcomes.
pitfalls: Attributing neonatal heart failure solely to a cardiac cause and omitting cranial imaging.
Emergency embolisation of a neonate with irreversible brain injury when comfort care is more appropriate.
Placing a ventriculoperitoneal shunt for hydrocephalus before addressing venous hypertension, which can worsen haemorrhage.
Underestimating pulmonary hypertension and its impact on peri-procedural stability.
Missing the diagnosis in an older infant presenting only with macrocephaly and delay.
